Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 57, verse 1:

﴿Everything in the heavens and the earth glorifies Allah﴾. This glorification mentioned here, and at the beginning of the other surahs that begin with glorification (al-musabbihat), may be literal, or it may be by the tongue of the state (lisan al-hal); for everything in the heavens and the earth is evidence of the existence of Allah, His power, and His wisdom. The first is more likely, because of His saying: ﴿But you do not understand their glorification﴾ [al-Isra: 44]. The mention of glorification here and in al-Hashr and al-Saff uses the past form sabbaha, while in al-Jumu'ah and al-Taghabun it uses the present form yusabbihu, and each of the two forms implies continuity.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 57, verse 3:

﴿He is the First and the Last﴾: that is, His existence has no beginning and His subsistence has no end. ﴿And the Outward and the Inward﴾: that is, the Outward is manifest to the intellects through the proofs and demonstrations that point to the Inward, which the eyes cannot perceive; or the Inward is that whose essence the intellects cannot reach to know. It has also been said: the Outward is the One who is high above everything, from your saying "I prevailed over (ẓahartu 'alā) the thing" when you rose above it; and the Inward is the One who knows the inner reality (bāṭin) of everything. The first interpretation is more apparent and more preferred. The conjunction "wa" (and) has been placed between these attributes to indicate that He, exalted is He, comprises them all, despite the difference in their meanings, and in this there is a verbal correspondence (muṭābaqa lafẓiyya), which is among the finest tools of eloquent expression.

[Qur'an 57:4] "Then He established Himself above the Throne." This has been discussed in Surah al-A'raf [7:53], and likewise what follows: "And He is with you wherever you are." It means that He is present with every person through His knowledge and His encompassing. The scholars have agreed on interpreting this verse in this way.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 57, verse 7:

﴿And spend of that in which He has made you successors﴾. It means spending in the way of Allah and in obedience to Him. It is narrated that it was revealed concerning spending for the expedition of Tabuk. In accordance with this, it is narrated that His words, "So those of you who believe and spend, for them is a great reward" [57:7], were revealed concerning ʿUthman ibn ʿAffan (may Allah be pleased with him), for he equipped the army of hardship (jaysh al-ʿusra) on that day. Nevertheless, the wording of the verse is general, and its ruling remains in force for all people. As for His words, "in which He has made you successors," it means that the wealth in your hands is in fact the wealth of Allah, since He created it; but He has granted you its use and made you successors (khulafaʾ) in disposing of it. Thus you are in the position of trustees (wukala'), so do not withhold it from spending in what its Owner has commanded you to spend it on. It is also possible that ﴿He has made you successors﴾ means successors to those who came before you, so that you inherited wealth from them; spend it before you leave it to those who come after you, just as those before you left it to you. The intent in every case is: an exhortation to spend and a discouragement from attachment to this world.

And what is it with you that you do not believe in God, when the Messenger calls you to believe, and when He has taken your covenant? (Translation of the passage follows.)

Let me give the translation properly:

"And what is [the matter] with you that you do not believe in God?" Its meaning: what thing prevents you from faith, when the Messenger calls you to it with decisive proofs and manifest miracles? So His saying "And what is [the matter] with you" is a question meant as a rebuke. And "you do not believe" is in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) relating to the verb implied by "what is with you."

In His saying "the Messenger calls you" and "and He has already taken your covenant" (mīthāqakum), this covenant may be the discernment placed in the intellects, which leads to faith, or it may be the covenant He took from the children of Adam, when He brought them out from the loins of Adam and made them bear witness concerning themselves: "Am I not your Lord?" They said: "Yes."

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 57, verse 9–10:

﴿He it is who sends down upon His servant clear signs﴾: he means our master Muhammad (ﷺ). The word "servant" (ʿabd) here is for honour and distinction, and "clear signs" (āyāt) here means the Qur'an. ﴿And what is [the matter] with you that you do not spend in the way of Allah﴾ to the end of the verse: its meaning is, what thing prevents you from spending in the way of Allah? And Allah inherits what is in the heavens and the earth when its people perish. In that there is an exhortation to spending and a discouragement from the world. ﴿Not equal among you are those who spent and fought before the conquest﴾. "The conquest" here is the conquest of Makkah, and it has been said it is the Treaty of Hudaybiyyah; the first is clearer and more well known. The meaning of the verse is a difference in reward and ranks, between those who spent in the way of Allah and fought before the conquest of Makkah, and those who spent and fought after it, for Islam before the conquest was weak, and the need for spending and fighting was more pressing. From the verse it is derived that whoever spends in a time of hardship has a greater reward than whoever spends in a time of ease. In the verse there is an ellipsis indicated by the context, its estimated meaning being: those among you who spent before the conquest and fought are not equal to those who spent after the conquest and fought. Then that was omitted because of the indication of His saying: ﴿They are greater in rank than those who spent afterwards and fought﴾. In this sense the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Do not revile my companions. For if one of you were to spend gold equal to Mount Uhud, it would not reach the mudd of one of them, nor half of it," meaning the foremost early ones among the Emigrants and the Helpers, and by this he addressed those who came after them from among the rest of the Companions; and every person who comes until the Day of Resurrection is included in the address. ﴿And to each Allah has promised the best [reward]﴾: that is, each of the two groups who spent and fought before the conquest and after it; Allah promised them Paradise.

﴿Who is it that will lend Allah a goodly loan?﴾ It has been mentioned in al-Baqara [2:245].

The governing element of the time adverb (العامل في الظرف) is أجر كريم (ajrun karīm, "a noble reward"), or an implied تقدير اذكر (taqdīr udhkur, "remember").

﴿On the day you see﴾ ﴿their light running before them and on their right hands﴾. It has been said that this light is a metaphor (isti'ārah) meaning guidance and divine pleasure. The sound view, that of the majority (al-jumhūr), is that it is literal (ḥaqīqah). This has been related from the Messenger of God (ﷺ). The meaning on this view is that on the Day of Resurrection the believers will have a light shining before them and to the right of each one of them.

It has also been said that its origin is in their right hands: they carry it, and its light spreads out in front of them. It is related that each person's light is according to the measure of his faith. Some will have a light like a palm tree, some will illuminate only what is near their feet, and some will shine at one moment and nearly go out at another. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "From this verse people derived the practice of a freed slave walking with a candle before his former master when the master dies."

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 57, verse 13:

﴿On the Day when the hypocrite men and the hypocrite women will say to those who believed, "Wait for us, that we may borrow from your light."﴾ ﴿On the Day﴾ is either a substitution (badal) for "the Day" in "the day you will see" (in the previous verse), or it is related to "the great triumph," or it is related to an elided verb whose sense is: "Remember."

The meaning of the verse is that every believer who manifests faith is given light on the Day of Resurrection. The light of the believers remains, while the light of the hypocrites is extinguished. So the hypocrites will say to the believers, ﴿"Wait for us, that we may borrow from your light."﴾ That is, we may take from it and be illuminated by it. The meaning of "wait for us" (unzurūnā) is "wait for us" (intaẓirūnā). This is because the believers hasten to Paradise like a flashing lightning, whereas the hypocrites are not like that. It is also possible that it derives from looking (naẓar), meaning "look at us," because when they look at them, they face them with their faces and are thereby illuminated by their light. But this is weak, because naẓar in the sense of looking with the eye is transitive with ilā (to). It has also been read unẓurūnā with a hamzah of cutting (hamzat qaṭʿ), and its meaning is "delay us," that is, give us respite in your walking until we catch up with you.

﴿It will be said, "Return behind you and seek light."﴾ This may be the speech of the believers, or the speech of the angels, and its meaning is rejection of the hypocrites and mockery of them, since they know that there is no light behind them. ﴿Behind you (warāʾakum)﴾ is an adverbial of place whose governing verb is ﴿return (ārjiʿū)﴾. It has also been said that it has no place in the grammatical structure (lā mawḍiʿa lahu min al-iʿrāb), and that it is as if one had said: "Return." The meaning of this return is: return to the place of standing and seek light there; or return to the world and seek light by attaining faith; or return disappointed and withdraw from us and seek another light, for there is no way for you to this light.

﴿So a wall with a gate will be struck between them.﴾ That is, a wall that separates them was set between the believers and the hypocrites, and in that wall is a gate for the people of Paradise to enter through. It has also been said that this wall is the Heights (al-Aʿrāf), which is a wall between Paradise and Hell. It has also been said that it is the eastern wall of Bayt al-Maqdis, but this is far-fetched. ﴿Its inner side has mercy, and its outer side faces the torment.﴾ Its inner side is the direction of the believers, and its outer side is the direction of the hypocrites, and it is external, like the saying "the outside of the city (ẓāhir al-madīna)," meaning outside it. The pronoun in "its inner side" and "its outer side" may refer to the wall or to the gate, and the first is more apparent.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 57, verse 14–15:

﴿They will call out to them: "Were we not with you?"﴾ That is, the hypocrites will call out to the believers and say to them: "Were we not with you in the world?" They mean to display their faith. ﴿"But you led yourselves into temptation (fatantum anfusakum)"﴾ That is, you destroyed them and led them astray by hypocrisy. ﴿"And you waited (wa-tarabbastum)"﴾ That is, you were slow with your faith. It was also said: you waited for the turns of fortune to befall the Prophet (ﷺ) and the Muslims. ﴿"And you doubted (wa-artabtum)"﴾ That is, you were in doubt about faith. ﴿"And false hopes deceived you (wa-gharrat-kumu al-amani)"﴾ That is, prolonged hope and wishful thinking. Among these is that they used to wish that the Prophet (ﷺ) and the believers would perish, or would be defeated, and other such false hopes. ﴿"Until the command of God came"﴾ That is, the conquest and the rise of Islam, or the death of the hypocrites in the state that brings punishment. ﴿"And the Deceiver (al-gharur) deceived you about God"﴾ The Deceiver is Satan. ﴿"It is your protector (mawlakum)"﴾ That is, it is more fitting for you, and the true meaning of mawla is the friend and helper, so this is a metaphor: you have no protector to turn to except the Fire.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 57, verse 16:

﴿Has not the time come for those who believe that their hearts should humble themselves to the remembrance of Allah﴾. The meaning of ﴿Has not the time come﴾: has it not drawn near. It is said: "anā al-amr" (anā al-amru) when the matter's appointed time has arrived. The remembrance of Allah may be taken to mean the Qur'an, or remembrance in general, or admonition with exhortations. This is a verse of admonition and reminder. Ibn ʿAbbas said: the believers were reproached with this verse thirteen years after the Qur'an had been revealed. Al-Fudayl ibn ʿIyad heard a reciter reciting this verse and said: "It has indeed come," and this was the cause of his return to Allah. It is related that ʿAbd Allah ibn al-Mubarak took up the lute (ʿud) in his youth to play it, but when it uttered this verse, Ibn al-Mubarak broke it and repented to Allah. ﴿And that they should not be like those who were given the Scripture before, ...﴾ This is coordinated (ʿataf) with "that they should humble themselves" by the phrase "and that they should not be," and it may be a prohibition. The intended meaning is a warning against the believers becoming like the People of the earlier Scriptures, namely the Jews and the Christians. ﴿So the term grew long for them﴾: that is, the span of life. It was said: waiting for the Resurrection. It was also said: waiting for victory. The first is more apparent.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 57, verse 17:

﴿Know that Allah gives life to the earth after its death﴾ That is, He gives it life by sending down rain and bringing forth vegetation. It was also said that this is an allegory for hearts, meaning: Allah gives life to hearts through admonitions just as He gives life to the earth through rain. In this there is consolation for the believers who were urged to let their hearts be humbled. The first meaning is more apparent and more preponderant, because it is the literal (ḥaqīqa) sense.

Indeed, those who give charity (*al-mutasaddiqin*, with the *sad* doubled) and the women who give charity. The original form is *al-mutasaddiqin*, and Ubayy ibn Ka'b read it this way. It is also read with a single *sad*, from *tasdiq* (affirmation), meaning that they affirmed the Messenger, peace be upon him.

﴿And lent to God﴾ is conjoined to the sense of the preceding clause, as if he had said: "Indeed those who gave charity and lent to God." We have already explained the meaning of *aqradu* (lent) in His words: ﴿Who is it that will lend to God?﴾ [al-Hadid: 11].

*Al-siddiqun* (those of great truthfulness) is an intensive form (*mubalaghah*) derived either from *sidq* (truthfulness) or from *tasdiq* (affirmation). That it derives from *sidq* is the stronger view, because the pattern *fi'il* (*fa'il* with a doubled middle radical, as in *siddiq*) is for the most part formed from a triliteral root. Its formation from a quadriliteral root has also been reported, as in the saying *rajul misik* (a miserly man), from *amsaka*.

﴿And the martyrs (*al-shuhada'*) with their Lord﴾ may be read in two ways. *Al-shuhada'* may be the subject (*mubtada'*), with its predicate being what follows. Or it may be conjoined (*ma'tuf*) to *al-siddiqun*.

If it is the subject, there are two views on its meaning. The first is that it is the plural of *shahid* (one who died in the way of God), and so He informs that they are with their Lord, and for them is their reward and their light. The second is that it is the plural of *shahid* (witness), meaning the prophets, peace be upon them, because they bear witness against their peoples.

If it is conjoined, there are also two views. The first is that it is the plural of *shahid* (martyr), and God describes the believers as being both *siddiqun* and *shuhada'*, that is, they combine the two attributes. It is related in this sense that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "The believers of my community are witnesses (*shuhada'*)," and then recited this verse. The second is that it is the plural of *shahid* (witness), because the believers bear witness over people, as in His words: ﴿That you may be witnesses over mankind﴾ [al-Baqarah: 143].

﴿For them is their reward and their light﴾: if *al-shuhada'* is the subject, this is a predicate about the martyrs specifically. If *al-shuhada'* is conjoined, it is a predicate about the believers. Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 57, verse 20:

﴿Like the rain whose vegetation pleases the tillers (al-kuffar)﴾ The meaning of the verse is a comparison of this world to crops that rain brings forth, which quickly change after their beauty, and are crushed after they have appeared. Here, "al-kuffar" (the tillers) is meant to refer to farmers, and it comes from His saying: "kafartu al-habba" (I covered the grain) when I hid it beneath the earth. He singled them out for mention because they are people of insight into crops and cultivation, so nothing pleases them except what truly deserves to please. It was also said: he meant the disbelievers in God, and He singled them out because they are more intensely impressed with this world and more eager for it.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 57, verse 21:

﴿Hasten to forgiveness from your Lord﴾. That is, hasten to the deeds by which you deserve forgiveness. It has been said: the meaning is, be in the first row in battle. It has been said: attend the opening takbir (takbir al-ihram) with the imam. It has been said: be the first to enter the mosque and the first to leave it. These are examples, and the general meaning is hastening to all righteous deeds. Some have cited this verse as evidence that praying at the beginning of the time is more excellent. ﴿And a Garden whose width is like the width of the heaven and the earth﴾. The word "heaven" here is intended to mean the category of heavens, as is shown by His saying in Ali 'Imran [133]. We have already explained the meaning of its width there.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 57, verse 22:

﴿No calamity befalls the earth or your own selves except that it is in a Book before We bring it into being.﴾ The meaning is that all matters are predestined and written in the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz) before they come to be. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Allah wrote the decrees of all things fifty thousand years before He created the heavens and the earth, and His Throne was upon the water." The word "calamity" (musibah) here refers to everything that befalls a person, whether good or bad. It was also said that it refers to calamity in the customary sense, which is what befalls one of evil, and it was specifically mentioned because it is of greatest concern to people. "In the earth" means droughts, earthquakes, and other such things; "in your selves" means death, poverty, and other such things. "Nabra'aha" means: We create it. The pronoun refers either to the calamity, or to "your selves," or to "the earth." It was also said that it refers to all of them, because the meaning is sound for each of them.

For the Qur'anic verse: "So that you do not despair over what has escaped you, nor exult over what He has given you."

The meaning: God did that and informed you of it, so that you would not grieve over what escaped you. The meaning of "la ta'saw" (do not grieve): do not be sad, i.e., do not grieve over what has escaped you of it, nor exult in it. The majority of readers recite "bima atakum" with the elongated alif (bi-ma ataakum), meaning "with what God has given you" of the world. Abu 'Amr recited "bima atakum" with the short alif, meaning "with what has come to you" of the world. If it is said: a person cannot control himself from rejoicing at good and grieving at evil, as Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (may God be pleased with him) said when a large amount of wealth was brought to him: "O God, we cannot help but rejoice in what You have adorned for us." The answer: the prohibition of rejoicing is only against that which leads to arrogance and tyranny, and against the grief that takes one out of patience and submission. "God does not love every arrogant boaster" (kulla mukhtalin fakhur). Al-mukhtal is the possessor of conceit, and al-fakhur is one who takes great pride over people.

﴿Those who withhold﴾ is either a substitute (بدل, *badal*, apposition) for every ﴿self-deluded boaster﴾ (كل مختار فخور, *kull mukhtal fakhur*), or the predicate (خبر, *khabar*) of an implied subject (مبتدأ, *mubtada'*), whose meaning is: "They are those who...". It may also be in the accusative by an implied verb, meaning: "I mean..." (أعني, *a'nī*). Or it may be a subject (مبتدأ) whose predicate is omitted (محذوف, *mahdhūf*).

Qur'anic quotations are rendered with the ﴿ ﴾ markers kept. Here is the translation.

﴿And We sent down with them the Book and the Balance﴾. "The Book" here is a generic term for the scriptures, and "the Balance" means justice. It was also said that "the Balance" refers to the instrument by which things are weighed. It is narrated that Jibril descended with the balance, gave it to Nuh, and said to him: "Command your people to weigh with it." ﴿And We sent down iron﴾. This is an informing about His creating it and bringing it into being through "sending down." It was also said: rather, He sent it down literally, because Adam descended from Paradise with the hammer and the needle. ﴿In it is great might﴾, meaning that weapons for fighting are made from it, and for this reason He said: "and that Allah may know who helps Him and His messengers unseen." And there are benefits for people: the ploughshares, the nails, and other things.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 57, verse 26:

﴿So among them is one who is guided, but many of them are defiantly disobedient﴾. That is: among the descendants of Nuh and Ibrahim there are few who are guided, and most of them are defiantly disobedient, because among them are the Jews, the Christians, and others.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 57, verse 27:

﴿Qaffaynā﴾ (We sent them following) is mentioned in al-Baqarah [87]. ﴿And We placed in the hearts of those who followed him compassion and mercy﴾. This is praise of them for the love some of them had for one another, just as the Companions of our master Muhammad (ﷺ) were described as ﴿merciful among themselves﴾. ﴿And monasticism, which they invented﴾. Rahbaniyyah (monasticism) is seclusion in the mountains, withdrawal from people into monasteries (sawami'), renouncing women and abandoning the world. The meaning of ibtada'uha (they invented it) is that they originated it without God having prescribed it for them. As for its grammatical analysis (i'rab), rahbaniyyah is conjoined (ma'tuf) to ra'fah and rahmah, meaning God placed in their hearts compassion, mercy and monasticism. Ibtada'uha is a descriptive clause (sifah) for rahbaniyyah, and al-ja'l (placing) here means al-khalq (creating). The Mu'tazilah parse rahbaniyyah as an object (maf'ul) of a suppressed verb which is explained by ibtada'uha, because their doctrine is that a person creates his own actions, so they parsed it according to their doctrine. Abu 'Ali al-Farisi also parsed it this way, and al-Zamakhshari mentioned both possibilities. ﴿We did not prescribe it for them, except in seeking the pleasure of God﴾. Kataba (prescribed) here means faradna (made obligatory) and shara'na (legislated). On this there are two opinions: first, that the exception (istithna') is disconnected (munqati'), and the meaning is that We did not prescribe monasticism for them, but they did it of their own accord, seeking the pleasure of God. Second, that the exception is connected (muttasil), and the meaning is that We prescribed it for them, seeking the pleasure of God. The first is more preferred, due to His saying "ibtada'uha" and due to the reading of 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud: "We did not prescribe it for them, but they invented it." ﴿But they did not observe it with its proper observance﴾. That is, they did not persist in it and did not guard it. They invented monasticism, and it was obligatory upon them to complete it, even though God the Exalted had not prescribed it for them, because whoever enters into a voluntary act of worship (nafl) must complete it. It was said: the pronoun refers to those who came after those who invented monasticism from among their followers.

O you who believe, believe in His Messenger. Here it may be asked: how does He address those who already believe and command them to believe, when obtaining what one already has is not fitting? The answer comes in two ways. The first is that the meaning of "believe" (āminū) is "persist in belief and remain steadfast upon it." The second is that the address is to the People of the Book, so the meaning is: O you who believed in Moses and Jesus, believe in Muhammad (ﷺ). This is supported by His words: ﴿He will give you a double portion of His mercy﴾, meaning two shares. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) also said: "Three will be given their reward twice: a man from the People of the Book who believed in his prophet and believed in me..." — the hadith continues.

﴿And He will make for you a light by which you will walk﴾. It may be that He means the light that will go before the believers on the Day of Resurrection, or that it is an expression for guidance. The first is supported by the fact that it is mentioned in this surah, and the second by His words: "And We made for him a light by which he walks among the people." ﴿So that the People of the Book may know that they have no power over anything of the bounty of Allah﴾. The "la" in "li-allā" is extra (ziyādah), and the meaning is: "so that the People of the Book may know." Thus Ibn ʿAbbās read it, and Ibn Masʿūd read "li-kayla yaʿlama" ("so that he may not know"). The meaning is: if the address is to the People of the Book, then: O People of the Book, believe in Muhammad (ﷺ), so that the People of the Book who did not believe in Muhammad (ﷺ) may know that they have no power over anything of the bounty of Allah, which He promised to those of you who believe, namely the multiplication of reward, the light, and forgiveness, because they did not submit and so they obtained none of that. If the address is to the Muslims, then the meaning is: so that the People of the Book who did not believe may know that they cannot obtain anything of what Allah has given the Muslims of multiplied reward, light, and forgiveness. It has also been narrated concerning the occasion of revelation of the verse that the Jews boasted over the Muslims, and the verse was revealed in refutation of them, and this strengthens this view. It is also narrated that its occasion was that those People of the Book who had embraced Islam boasted over other Muslims that Allah would give them their reward twice, so the verse was revealed informing them that the Muslims are equal to them in that.
